clusters.neutral_headline: My week wearing ankle weights: 'I was helping kickstart my muscles'

items.title: My week wearing ankle weights: 'I was helping kickstart my muscles'
items.standfirst: When a knee injury forced me to change my fitness routine, I added Sportneer ankle weights – and got a decent workoutI’m a personal trainer. Here’s the equipment I useSign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better thingsMy exercise regimen has changed drastically over the last 15 years. A self-confessed cardio queen in my 20s and 30s, I alternated days at the gym with dance and Hiit classes and endured long bouts on the full complement of cardio equipment. And then my body caught up with me. First it was bursitis in my knee, which my doctor called “burpee-itis” from the ridiculous amount of the exercises I was performing. “You have to listen to your body,” he lightly chided as he poked at my swollen kneecap. Once my lower back started to complain, I had to start making serious concessions.Thankfully, finding new ways to stay in shape was not as hard as I thought. A quick pivot led me to strength training, barre and pilates classes, and lots and lots of walking. My knee was still keeping me from doing a ton of basic leg work including squats and lunges, so ankle weights seemed like an easy solution. After doing some research on what would fit my specific needs, I decided on Sportneer ankle weights and used them daily for a week to see if they could enhance my lower body workouts. Continue reading...

clusters.title: Palantir patient data tech rejected by many NHS trusts in England
clusters.neutral_headline: Palantir patient data tech rejected by many NHS trusts in England

items.title: Palantir patient data tech rejected by many NHS trusts in England
items.standfirst: Exclusive: health bodies across country say controversial US firm’s data platform no better than systems already in useNHS organisations that care for millions of people in England are rejecting Palantir’s patient data technology, according to freedom of information responses that reveal health bosses believe they can find better or equal alternatives in many cases.Some health bodies said the £330m federated data platform (FDP) operated by the controversial US company had made it easier to manage waiting lists and has improved surgery scheduling. But, from Gateshead to Truro, others said they were declining to use it or had carried out trials and reverted to old systems. A Suffolk trust said other systems “supercede” the FDP’s functionality, while Greater Manchester’s care board called the Palantir system “duplicative” and “retrograde”. Continue reading...

clusters.title: The Letby case inquiry will lead to more blame and suspicion in the NHS – and patients will be less safe | Mark McDonald
clusters.neutral_headline: The Letby case inquiry will lead to more blame and suspicion in the NHS – and...

items.title: The Letby case inquiry will lead to more blame and suspicion in the NHS – and patients will be less safe | Mark McDonald
items.standfirst: I fear for what comes next because medics must be able to ask questions, raise concerns and admit mistakes. A defensive staff is dangerous for everyoneMark McDonald is a barrister representing Lucy LetbyI have been Lucy Letby’s barrister for the past two years. I have spent thousands of hours going through the evidence, speaking to experts and examining what happened to the babies who died or became seriously unwell on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester hospital. I have worked with nearly 30 experts, including internationally recognised specialists in neonatology, pathology, insulin, statistics and other fields. It may be to some an inconvenient truth, but I am convinced that Letby is innocent, and her convictions represent one of the most serious miscarriages of justice in modern British legal history. That means she was failed by the police, the NHS, the criminal justice system and, importantly, a plethora of experts who simply got it wrong.My work on the case has also raised wider concerns about the evidence and conclusions surrounding the deaths on the neonatal unit, and what the lessons being drawn from this case will mean for doctors and nurses in neonatal medicine.Mark McDonald is a criminal defence and human rights barrister specialising in miscarriages of justiceDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
